nameStory: This bee gets its 'rotund' name from its pleasantly plump, rounded body shape that makes it look like a tiny flying marble. The 'resin' part comes from its fascinating habit of collecting sticky tree sap and plant resins to build and waterproof its nest chambers. 'Northern' simply indicates it's the cold-hardy member of its group, adapted to survive New England's harsh winters.
description: The Northern Rotund Resin Bee is a small, stocky native bee that looks like a miniature bumblebee but with a more compact, rounded body. These solitary bees are typically dark-colored with subtle light markings and reach about the size of a small fingernail. Unlike honeybees that live in hives, each female works alone to build her own nest using collected plant resins. They're part of the mason bee family, known for their skilled construction abilities.

idTips.label: Body Shape
idTips.description: Distinctly rounded and compact body that appears almost ball-like, much more rotund than typical bees with their elongated abdomens

idTips.label: Size
idTips.description: Small bee, roughly 6-8mm long, about the size of a small fingernail or peppercorn

idTips.label: Coloration
idTips.description: Generally dark brown to black with subtle pale yellow or white markings, lacking the bright stripes of honeybees

idTips.label: Flight Pattern
idTips.description: Quick, darting flight with frequent hovering near flowers or potential nest sites, often appears to bounce through the air

idTips.label: Behavior
idTips.description: Often seen collecting sticky substances from pine trees or other resinous plants, may appear to be 'mining' bark or plant stems

idTips.label: Nest Sites
idTips.description: Look for small holes in wood, plant stems, or existing cavities that appear sealed with dark, shiny resin that feels hard and smooth to touch

habitat: Northern Rotund Resin Bees prefer areas with abundant flowering plants near sources of tree resin, such as mixed forests with pine, spruce, or fir trees. They're commonly found in forest edges, parks, and gardens where they can access both nectar sources and resinous materials. Look for them in areas with dead wood, hollow plant stems, or existing beetle holes they can use as nest sites.

seasonality.spring: Adults emerge from overwintering sites in late spring and begin foraging on early flowers. This is when you're most likely to spot them actively collecting resin from trees.
seasonality.summer: Peak activity period when females are busy provisioning nests with pollen and nectar. Look for them visiting a variety of flowers and working on nest construction.
seasonality.fall: New generation completes development inside resin-sealed nest chambers. Adults may still be active on warm days visiting late-season flowers before finding overwintering sites.
seasonality.winter: Adults overwinter in protected locations like hollow stems or wood crevices. Nests remain sealed with hardened resin until spring emergence.

funFact: These ingenious bees are nature's original caulk contractors — they collect sticky tree resin that hardens into a waterproof, antiseptic seal for their nest chambers, creating what's essentially a natural preservative that keeps their developing young safe from moisture and harmful bacteria for months!
confusionNotes: Most likely confused with small dark mason bees or mining bees, but the Northern Rotund Resin Bee's distinctly round, ball-like body shape sets it apart from the more elongated profiles of similar species. Memory trick: 'Rotund and round' — if it looks like a tiny flying marble, it's probably your resin bee.
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called a 'resin bee,' these insects don't produce resin themselves — they're skilled collectors and recyclers of natural tree saps and sticky plant substances. The family name Megachilidae means 'large-lipped,' referring to their prominent mandibles used for cutting and manipulating nesting materials.
compareHints: Since this is the only Anthidiellum species recorded in New England, compare it with other small mason bees in the Megachilidae family. Northern Rotund Resin Bees are noticeably more compact and rounded than related Osmia mason bees, which have more typical elongated bee proportions. They're also smaller than most leafcutter bees and lack the distinctive large mandibles of Megachile species.
